7563.d:
The Mandelbrot set is a fractal derived by repeatedly applying the equation f(z) = z*z + c over the 2D space of complex numbers. From this simple equation emerges a realm of beautiful and surprisingly organic looking shapes.

Fractal Reef offers a meditation on the emergence of life-like complexity from simple processes. I've animated the Mandelbrot by injecting noise into various points into the calculation. Each generated version opens a tiny window onto the immense form. In one or two, you can still see the characteristic beetle shape of the Mandelbrot.

While the dominant dimensions of noise will create tide-like movements, no token is likely to repeat a loop point for many millions of years. The animation is driven by the real-world time. Assuming your clock is accurate, you're unlikely to ever see the exact same image twice.

7578.d:
‘tur1ng’ consists of audible image architectures based on the principle of Turing machines. These systems are mathematical models of computation that manipulate symbols on a strip of tape according to a table of rules. The machine first writes a symbol in a cell on the tape, then either moves the tape one cell left or right, then, based on the observed symbol and the machine's own state in the table, either proceeds to another instruction or halts computation.

In ‘tur1ng’, rules are stored as colors and the original tape cells are constructed from a two dimensional array. The sound unfolds as the algorithm proceeds: monitoring these binary songs requires being attentive to changes in the state or behavior of the system over time so that appropriate interventions or other process-related activities may be carried out. Another feature of listening algorithms is that it often has to be done as a background or secondary task or, perhaps, in parallel with one or more other primary tasks.

Touch to listen.

7600.d:
I've long found myself interested in systems where the rules are simple, but non-linear interactions between system elements lead to difficult to predict behaviors.

In 'Spin Cycle' the rules are as simple as can be. Individuals navigate along a path. When they exit a tile, that tile rotates.

In a world with a single individual, the future is solely a function of its own behaviors. Yet still we find it can be difficult to predict too far forward.

As the community grows, the potential for one individual's behaviors to affect the path of another grows alongside it. The result is a future that is increasingly difficult to know up until it has arrived.

Features:

- grid size: how many tiles
- individuals: how many individuals
- paths: curved or straight
- background: what is drawn behind the paths
- blackholes: cause unsuspecting agents to disappear

Certain keys can be pressed to adjust what gets rendered.

7632.d:
This GT is based on the Gumowski-Mira chaotic attractor.
A particular variant was called "Mythic Bird" due to its similarity to feathered wings.

The code to generate this is minimal:

X=0.01,Y=0
G=()=>M*X+2*(1-M)*X*X/(1+X*X)
for(I=N;I>0;I--)
{
  plot(W/2+X*SCALEX,H/2+Y*SCALEY)
  Z=X,X=Y+G()+A*(1-B*Y*Y)*Y,Y=-Z+G()
}

The co-efficients A, B and M decide the final shape.

“Les Vampires” is a bw 1915–16 French silent crime serial film written and directed by Louis Feuillade. It is a magical masterpiece with impact on great directors like Luis Bunuel, Fritz Lang and Alfred Hitchcock… In the film, a reporter and his friend battle a secret society of criminals; “The Vampires”… 

The face used here, is an off-shoot of the vampire from the film; Irma Vep. Irma Vep is played by the French actress/director/writer Jeanne Roques aka Musidora. The caharacter inspired Vampyra, Cat Woman and many other contemporary “Goths” like Siouxsie Sioux and Courtney Love.

“Although vice is seldom punished, virtue is always rewarded.”

Elsewhere I do video/photo manipulations, illustrations and here, I do collages that are built on masks/faces from relevant masterpieces of cinema. Overall; I use masks, personas, glitch, reflections, shadows and I am intrigued by fauxtography and the doppelganger theory.

7680.d:
In the footsteps of Euclid, Adolf Zeising and Leonardo Fibonacci. The golden number Phi 1.6180339. 

The beginning forms a square, which is divided with the rules of the golden ratio. The partition is done on the left, right, top or bottom side. Where to divide, is decided by chance.Two rectangles are created. The process repeats. The rectangles are partitioned again according to the described rules.

The algorithm allows between 6 and 250 divisions. The number of the divisions is also random. With just 6 divisions an image of 4096 possible variants is created. At only 20 divisions there are 1,099,511,627,776 variants.

There are 29 different color palettes. After the division a random assignment takes place. A color palette consists of at least 4 colors. Which color each of the rectangles gets, is again decided by chance.

Features:
* 29 color palettes
* 5 division levels
* 4 background colors
* black/white grain

By pressing the numbers 1-4 on the keyboard, the image can be saved in a resolution up to 8K.

As well transparencies(especially applied to the white areas).

Inspired by the architecture of my hometown church, I studied some other churches and cathedrals I came with the idea of generating fictional buildings.

There are 3 styles: the original made with colourful bricks, the second entirely made out of lines and the last mostly made out of rectangles.

Some animation: the light of the windows turns off randomly, the colours of the clocks and bricks change and the clock is updated to your local time.

Controls:
* Press "s" to save the current image
* Press "h" to stop the animation
* Press "r" to resume the animation

Features:
* color scheme: 20 variations of sets of 4 colours
* style: default, line or cubic
* blocks: number of blocks, between 5 and 15
* crosses: number of crosses, between 0 and 5
* gates: number of gates, between 0 and 5
* roofs: number of roofs, between 0 and 5
* windows: number of windows, between 0 and  15

Made in Zoutleeuw, Belgium by Gorik with p5.

7739.d:
The Library of Babel consists of an enormous expanse of adjacent hexagonal rooms. In each room are four walls of bookshelves. Though the order and content of the books are random and apparently completely meaningless, the books contain every possible ordering of 25 basic characters (22 letters, the period, the comma, and space). Though the vast majority of the books in this universe are pure gibberish, the library also must contain, somewhere, every coherent book ever written, or that might ever be written. The library contains all useful information, including predictions of the future. Because of this glut of information, most books are totally useless to the reader.

Each iteration represents one page of 410, in one book of 32, on one shelf of 5, on one wall of 4, in the endless expanse of hexagonal rooms within the Library of Babel.

Gradient Text: 1 in 10 chance
Gradient Title: 1 in 100 chance
Gradient Background: 1 in 1000 chance

Based upon the fiction of Jorge Luis Borges

7740.d:
This generative token explores redundancy as an architectural concept, method, and process. Redundancy provides flexibility in an open form, enabling a shift from monofunctional to multifunctional as well as from optimized to resilient. A hybrid architecture in which complexity is created through the continuous reconfiguration of simple discrete and compatible blocks.
Each minted redundancy token reveals various deterministic rare features, styles, and scales, creating endlessly redundant open architectures. 

Redundancy Generative Token by @grasser_alex 2022

7743.d: A square composed of horizontal lines appears taller and narrower than an identical square made up of vertical lines. Reporting this illusion, Hermann von Helmholtz noted that such illusions, in which such a space seems to be larger than an unfilled space, were common in everyday life, adding the observation that dresses with horizontal stripes are believed to make the figure look taller. We find that a rectangle of vertical stripes needs to be extended by 7.1% vertically to match the height of a square of horizontal stripes and that a rectangle of horizontal stripes must be made 4.5% wider than a square of vertical stripes to match its perceived width. This illusion holds when the horizontal or vertical lines are on the dress of a line drawing of a woman, even though that's a bit sexist.
